Case_Name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
Title: Notice of Appearance & Arrest Guidelines
Holding_Text: Police officers cannot arrest an accused person mechanically or automatically for offences where the maximum punishment is imprisonment for 7 years or less (e.g. Section 85/86 BNS / Section 498A IPC, theft, cheating). Instead, police must mandatorily serve a Notice of Appearance under Section 35 of the BNSS (formerly Section 41A of CrPC) requiring appearance before the investigating officer. Arrest can only be made if the accused fails to comply or if the police officer records specific statutory reasons in writing justifying custody.

Case_Name: Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P.
Title: Mandatory Registration of First Information Report (FIR)
Holding_Text: Registration of a First Information Report (FIR) is strictly mandatory under Section 173 BNSS (formerly Section 154 CrPC) if the information disclosed to the police discloses the commission of a cognizable offence. Police officers have no discretion to refuse registration or conduct preliminary inquiries before registering the FIR in cognizable matters, except in limited categories like commercial disputes, matrimonial discord, medical negligence, or corruption cases where a preliminary inquiry must be concluded within 14 days.

Title: Categorization of Offences and Bail Guidelines
Holding_Text: The Supreme Court classified offences into four distinct categories (A, B, C, D) for streamlined bail adjudication. For Category A offences (punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years), bail should ordinarily be granted on appearance before the court without taking the accused into custody, provided the accused was not arrested during investigation and cooperated. The court reiterated that bail is the rule and jail is the exception.

Case_Name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
Title: Arrestee Fundamental Rights and Safeguards Against Custodial Violence
Holding_Text: The Supreme Court laid down 11 mandatory guidelines to protect citizens against custodial violence and torture: 1) Police personnel carrying out arrest must wear clear identification and name tags; 2) An arrest memo must be prepared at the time of arrest and attested by at least one witness (family member or respectable citizen); 3) The arrestee has the absolute right to have a friend, relative, or well-wisher informed of the arrest and place of custody within 8 to 12 hours; 4) The arrestee must be medically examined at the time of arrest and re-examined every 48 hours by a trained doctor; 5) The arrestee is permitted to meet their advocate during interrogation.

Case_Name: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
Title: Fundamental Right to Privacy & Informational Autonomy
Holding_Text: A nine-judge Constitutional Bench unanimously ruled that the Right to Privacy is a fundamental right protected under Article 21 and Part III of the Constitution of India. Privacy encompasses spatial privacy, bodily autonomy, and informational privacy (data protection). Any law or state action infringing upon privacy must satisfy a threefold test: 1) Legality (backed by a valid law); 2) Legitimate state aim; and 3) Proportionality (ensuring the least restrictive intrusion).

Case_Name: Dashrath Rupsingh Rathod v. State of Maharashtra
Title: Territorial Jurisdiction for Section 138 Cheque Dishonour Complaints
Holding_Text: Following this judgment and the subsequent 2015 statutory amendment to Section 142(2) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, a complaint for dishonour of cheque under Section 138 can only be filed before the court within whose local jurisdiction the bank branch is situated where the payee (complainant) maintains the bank account where the cheque was presented for clearance. If the cheque is presented for payment over the counter, jurisdiction lies where the drawer's account is maintained.

Title: Involuntary Narco-Analysis, Polygraph and Brain Mapping Prohibited
Holding_Text: The Supreme Court held that compulsory administration of narco-analysis, polygraph (lie-detector) tests, and brain electrical activation profiling (BEAP) on an accused person violates the fundamental right against self-incrimination guaranteed under Article 20(3) and the right to privacy and dignified life under Article 21. No citizen can be subjected to involuntary lie-detector or narco tests without their informed and recorded consent before a Magistrate.

Applicable_Statute: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
Title: Comprehensive Guidelines on Maintenance and Financial Disclosure
Holding_Text: The Supreme Court mandated that in all matrimonial disputes claiming maintenance under the Domestic Violence Act, Hindu Marriage Act, or Section 125 CrPC / BNSS, both the applicant wife and respondent husband must file a comprehensive Affidavit of Assets and Liabilities. Maintenance must be awarded from the date of filing the application and must ensure a standard of living consistent with the status enjoyed during the matrimonial cohabitation.
